title: Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to translate the philosophical concept of meaningful human control into practical design guidance for AI systems. The authors argue that as AI systems become more autonomous, opaque, and embedded in complex socio-technical environments, responsibility gaps can arise unless systems are designed so that humans can remain meaningfully in control and morally responsible for outcomes.

The paper proposes four actionable properties for AI system development: an explicit moral operational design domain (moral ODD), appropriate and mutually compatible representations between humans and AI agents, alignment between responsibility, ability, and authority to control the system, and explicit links between AI actions and the decisions of humans who are aware of their moral responsibility. These properties are developed through abductive thinking and illustrated with two non-education case studies: automated vehicles and AI-based hiring.

The paper does not study a student population or an educational intervention. Instead, it offers a theoretical framework meant to support designers, developers, and other stakeholders in building AI systems that facilitate meaningful human control across the system lifecycle. The authors conclude that the four properties are necessary design anchors, though not sufficient by themselves to ensure ethical AI overall, and that transdisciplinary socio-technical practices are needed to operationalize them in specific contexts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing actionable properties for meaningful human control in AI systems. It does not present an empirical study, comparison, or outcome evaluation in K-12 education.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention is tested and no student, teacher, or system outcome is measured. The paper is relevant only as a governance/design framework, not as evidence of impact.
